articles.title: COP31's "35 by 35" Plan: Is More Electricity Always Cleaner?
articles.dek: Türkiye wants electricity to supply 35% of the world's energy by 2035, but the pledge does not say where that electricity must come from.
paras: When world leaders arrived in Antalya, Türkiye, this week for COP31, the United Nations climate conference running from 9 to 20 November, the host country placed one idea at the top of the agenda: electricity. Türkiye, which holds the presidency, is promoting a pledge known as "35 by 35". It asks countries to raise electricity's share of the world's final energy consumption from roughly one-fifth today to 35% by 2035. The idea sounds technical, but it has quickly become one of the most debated proposals at the summit.

To understand the target, it helps to know how the world actually uses energy. Most energy is not consumed as electricity at all. Cars burn petrol, many homes are heated by gas boilers, and factories burn coal or gas to produce heat. Electrification means replacing these machines with electric versions, such as electric vehicles, heat pumps and electric furnaces. Because electric motors and heat pumps waste far less energy than engines and boilers, the same tasks can be done with less total energy. According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), transport, buildings and industry account for about 45% of direct global greenhouse gas emissions, and electrifying them could cut those emissions by 40% by 2035.

Supporters argue that the pledge offers two benefits at once. The first is climate protection. Australia's climate minister, Chris Bowen, who is leading the negotiations, has said the world has "no chance" of holding warming to 1.5°C without reaching the 35% mark. The second is energy security. This year, disruption to oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz has driven up fuel prices around the world. COP31 president Murat Kurum argues that countries which import oil and gas have little control over their own energy, whereas electricity can be generated at home. The IEA estimates that wider electrification could reduce global oil demand by 18 million barrels a day.

There is also a diplomatic logic. At COP30 in Brazil last year, efforts to agree on a roadmap away from fossil fuels collapsed amid opposition from several major producers. Talking about expanding electricity, rather than abolishing oil, gas and coal, is far less divisive. This may explain why the pledge has attracted backers such as the European Union, the United Kingdom and Canada. However, the pledge is voluntary, and each country keeps "full authority" over its own policies. France, among others, would prefer a formal COP decision that carries more weight.

Critics point to a serious weakness: the pledge does not require the extra electricity to come from clean sources. About one-third of the world's electricity is still generated by burning coal. If a country replaces petrol cars with electric ones but charges them with coal power, the climate gains shrink considerably, and new coal or gas plants built to meet rising demand could stay in operation for decades. Sceptics warn that this would lock in fossil fuel use rather than end it. Meanwhile, oil and gas producers such as Saudi Arabia argue that fossil fuels can remain a large part of the energy mix if emissions are captured.

The numbers show how much depends on this detail. Renewable sources supplied about 31.7% of global electricity in 2024. Meeting the 35% target with mostly renewable power would require that share to reach roughly 78% by 2035. Analysts quoted by ABC News estimate that meeting the target with clean energy alone could reduce projected warming by about 0.3°C, from a path of at least 2.6°C under current policies. More than 90 campaign groups have welcomed the target, but they want safeguards guaranteeing that new demand is met with renewable power.

Even supporters admit that the practical obstacles are enormous. Electricity must travel through grids, and many grids are already overloaded, with thousands of renewable projects waiting to be connected. The International Renewable Energy Agency has described networks as "structurally unprepared" for electrification on this scale. Investment in grids and storage would need to double, from about $500 billion in 2025 to $1 trillion a year. Poorer countries face the hardest task, since many must build or rebuild their grids almost from scratch, and the campaign group Global Witness warns that shortages of minerals such as copper could slow progress.

Is the "35 by 35" pledge a breakthrough or a distraction? The answer may depend less on the number itself than on what fills the gap. A world that runs more of its cars, homes and factories on clean electricity would almost certainly be cooler and less vulnerable to oil shocks. A world that simply burns more coal to produce that electricity would not. As delegates bargain in Antalya, the real test of the pledge will be whether the extra power is clean, affordable and fairly shared.

speak.p: Some people think governments should make citizens switch to electric cars and electric heating as soon as possible. Others think people should be free to choose when to switch. Which view do you agree with? Use specific reasons and examples.
speak.hint: State your view → reason 1 (climate/energy security or cost/fairness) + example → reason 2 + example → short conclusion.

write.p: Professor: This week at COP31, Türkiye is promoting a pledge to raise electricity's share of global energy use to 35% by 2035. Supporters say it is a practical goal that most countries can agree on. Critics say it is meaningless unless the extra electricity is clean. In your view, should the pledge require that new electricity come from renewable sources, even if that means fewer countries sign it? Why or why not? (Lena says: Yes, it should. If countries can meet the target by burning more coal, the pledge may actually make climate change worse, because new power plants run for decades. A weaker pledge with many signatures only looks successful.) (Omar says: I disagree. Poorer countries need cheap electricity now, and they cannot build solar and wind farms overnight. A flexible pledge gets everyone moving in the right direction, and the power supply can be cleaned up step by step later.)
steps: Choose a side: require clean power, or keep the pledge flexible.
Give one reason linked to emissions or fairness.
Add an example, such as new coal plants running for decades or a poor country without a grid.
Respond to Lena or Omar, then conclude in one sentence.

articles.title: Meta Uses AI to Guess Users' Ages: Protection or Privacy Risk?
articles.dek: Instagram will now move suspected teenagers into restricted accounts even if they claim to be adults. Is a computer's guess about your age a safeguard or an intrusion?

sources.name: Anadolu Agency via A News, Nov 9, 2026

paras: Anyone who has signed up for a social media account knows how easy it is to lie about one's age: a user simply types in a false birthday. On 9 November, Meta, the company that owns Instagram, Facebook and Threads, announced that it will no longer rely only on that birthday. The company is expanding an artificial intelligence (AI) system that estimates users' ages to Instagram accounts worldwide. If the system suspects that a user is a teenager, the account will be moved into a more restrictive "Teen Account", even if the person registered as an adult.

Teen Accounts were introduced to answer growing criticism that social media harms young people. They limit who can contact a teenager, filter the content teenagers see and encourage them to spend less time on the app. The problem is that these protections only work if the platform knows who is a teenager. Meta first used AI age estimation in the United States, the United Kingdom, Canada and Australia, before extending it to Brazil and the 27 member states of the European Union in May. Facebook is now receiving the same technology, and a global launch on Threads is planned for later this year.

Meta has not explained in detail which signals its system uses. Earlier this year, however, the company said its tools could examine visual cues in photos and videos that users have already posted, such as height and bone structure, to estimate a broad age range rather than an exact age. Meta stressed that this was "not facial recognition", because the system does not try to match a face to a person's identity. Instead, it makes a statistical guess about whether the person in the images is likely to be a child, a teenager or an adult.

The expansion did not happen in a vacuum. Meta faces intense legal and political pressure in the United States, where it has reached an agreement with 52 attorneys general from states, territories and the District of Columbia to improve how it identifies teenagers and children under 13. As part of the rollout, parents in the US will see a video in their Instagram feed this month explaining the system and how to make sure their children give accurate ages. For a company accused of putting profits before children's safety, the change allows Meta to show regulators that it is taking action.

Supporters of the move argue that self-reported birthdays have always been an empty safeguard. A thirteen-year-old who claims to be twenty can avoid every protection designed for her age group. From this point of view, an imperfect AI estimate is still better than a rule that anyone can bypass in seconds. Child-safety advocates have long demanded that platforms take responsibility for knowing their users, rather than shifting the entire burden onto parents.

Critics, however, raise several concerns. First, Meta has published no accuracy figures, so outsiders cannot tell how often adults are wrongly labelled as teenagers or how many teenagers slip through. A 2024 evaluation by the US National Institute of Standards and Technology found that no single age-estimation algorithm clearly outperformed the others, and that results varied with image quality, age, sex and country of birth. Second, the announcement does not describe how misclassified users can challenge a decision or how long the data generated by the system will be kept. Analysing people's bodies in photos, even without identifying them, may also raise concerns about biometric data.

There is a practical complication as well: the person in a photo is not always the account holder. Australia's eSafety Commissioner found that 54% of children aged eight to twelve who used social media did so through a parent's or carer's account. Meta itself argues that a better solution would be a single age signal provided by the device or the app store. In Australia, it has begun using an age-range signal supplied by Apple, and it has urged rivals such as TikTok and YouTube to adopt similar methods so that protections are consistent across platforms.

The debate reflects a wider dilemma of the digital age. Protecting children online seems to require platforms to know more about their users, yet collecting more information creates new risks to privacy. Meta's AI may well shield millions of teenagers from unwanted contact and harmful content. Whether the public accepts it, however, will depend on questions the company has not yet fully answered: how accurate the system is, how mistakes can be corrected, and who controls the data it produces.

write.p: Professor: Meta is now using AI to estimate the ages of Instagram users around the world and to move suspected teenagers into restricted accounts, even if they claimed to be adults. Some people welcome this as a long-overdue protection. Others worry about privacy and mistakes. Do you think social media companies should use AI to estimate users' ages? Why or why not? (Mia says: Yes. Anyone can type a fake birthday in seconds, so the old system protects nobody. If AI can stop strangers from contacting a twelve-year-old, a few annoyed adults is a small price to pay.) (Daniel says: I'm not convinced. The company hasn't said how accurate the AI is or how to appeal. Letting a private company analyse our photos to judge our age gives it even more power over our personal data.)
steps: Decide: support AI age checks, or oppose them.

articles.title: Roads Kill Nearly One in Five of California's Mountain Lions Each Year
articles.dek: A new report says traffic is now the deadliest threat to California's pumas. Are famous wildlife bridges the answer, or do simple fences matter more?
paras: Mountain lions, also known as pumas or cougars, are among the most powerful predators in North America. Yet in California, the greatest danger they face is not a rival animal or a hunter, but a car. According to the 2026 California Roadkill Hotspots Report, released on 10 November by the Road Ecology Center at the University of California, Davis, vehicle collisions kill about 18% of the state's mountain lion population every year, at least 780 animals.

The report is based on the California Roadkill Observation System, a database containing about 235,000 records of animals killed on roads, covering 77 amphibian, 388 bird, 112 reptile and 193 mammal species. Much of this information comes from observers who report dead animals and where they found them. The researchers stress that their figures are almost certainly underestimates, since the data cover only around half of California's roads. The true number of deaths is probably considerably higher.

Mountain lions are not the only victims. Vehicles kill roughly 9.5% of California's mule deer, around 44,000 animals a year. That is two to four times as many deer as hunters take. For a common species such as the mule deer, these losses are serious but survivable. For mountain lions, which reproduce slowly and need very large territories, the impact is far greater.

The report identifies hotspots where collisions cluster, including sections of Interstates 280 and 15, State Routes 62 and 118, and US Highway 101. The damage is proportionally greatest in southern and central coastal California, where mountain lion populations are small and have recently been listed as threatened under the California Endangered Species Act. In these areas, highways act like walls. Lions that try to cross are often killed, while those that stay behind can become trapped in shrinking, isolated groups that lose genetic diversity.

The most famous response to this problem is the Wallis Annenberg Wildlife Crossing, a huge bridge over US Highway 101 near Los Angeles that is described as the largest wildlife crossing in the world. It is due to open on 2 December, and a camera has already photographed a coyote using it. Projects like this capture the public imagination, and supporters argue that they show drivers and politicians that wild animals deserve space too.

However, the report's authors argue that crossings alone are not enough. "Fencing is the answer to reducing roadkill, not crossings alone," said Fraser Shilling, director of the Road Ecology Center. A bridge does not guarantee that animals will use it; without fences to guide them, many will still try to cross the road directly. The report therefore recommends fencing roadkill hotspots and the land beside existing passages, such as creek tunnels and small road underpasses, which animals already use. It even names the Liberty Canyon underpass, right next to the new crossing, as a priority for fencing.

Fencing is not a perfect solution either. Fences that are not paired with safe passages can turn a dangerous road into a complete barrier, cutting populations off from mates and food. Building and maintaining long stretches of fencing also costs money that transport agencies might prefer to spend on roads. Yet collisions have costs too: crashes with large animals damage vehicles and injure drivers, and an earlier report from the same centre estimated that wildlife-vehicle collisions cost California at least $1 billion over five years. The new report also calls for fresh crossings where animals still migrate, such as Interstate 8 near the Mexican border.

Shilling has warned that unless California invests in extensive fencing, or reduces traffic volumes and speeds, the state will "continue to see declines" in iconic animals such as pumas and deer. The findings raise a question that reaches far beyond California. As roads spread across the planet, how much are societies willing to pay, in money and in convenience, to share the landscape with wild animals?

words.def: an animal that kills and eats other animals

words.def: an accident in which a moving vehicle or object hits something
words.ex: Thick fog caused a collision between two buses on the bridge.

words.def: a number or amount that is lower than the real one
words.ex: The figure of 200 visitors was an underestimate; nearly 300 people came.

words.def: to produce young animals or plants
words.ex: Some turtles reproduce only once every few years.

words.def: an area that an animal treats as its own and defends against others
words.ex: A single tiger may patrol a territory of more than 50 square kilometres.

words.def: to gather or happen close together in one place
words.ex: Small shops tend to cluster around the train station.

words.def: separated from others, so that contact is difficult
words.ex: The isolated village had no road until 1995.

keySentences.text: Yet in California, the greatest danger they face is not a rival animal or a hunter, but a car.
keySentences.note: The 'not ... but' structure gives the surprising main point. TOEFL often tests contrasts introduced by 'Yet'.

keySentences.text: The researchers stress that their figures are almost certainly underestimates, since the data cover only around half of California's roads.
keySentences.note: 'Almost certainly' and 'since' show the researchers' caution and their reason. Questions often ask why a figure may be unreliable.

keySentences.text: Lions that try to cross are often killed, while those that stay behind can become trapped in shrinking, isolated groups that lose genetic diversity.
keySentences.note: This sentence explains two separate harms of highways. It is tested as a sentence-simplification question.

keySentences.text: A bridge does not guarantee that animals will use it; without fences to guide them, many will still try to cross the road directly.
keySentences.note: This challenges the popular idea that wildlife bridges solve the problem. The semicolon links a claim to its explanation.

keySentences.text: Fencing is not a perfect solution either.
keySentences.note: The author now gives the other side. 'Either' signals that neither crossings nor fences are perfect.

keySentences.text: As roads spread across the planet, how much are societies willing to pay, in money and in convenience, to share the landscape with wild animals?
keySentences.note: The passage ends with a wider question, inviting readers to weigh costs and benefits beyond California.

questions.q: The word "take" in paragraph 3 is closest in meaning to
opts: carry away from a place
need
accept
kill or catch
questions.why: The sentence compares deer killed by vehicles with deer killed by hunters, so 'take' here means kill or catch.
questions.evidence: That is two to four times as many deer as hunters take.
optWhy: Another meaning of the word: 'take a bag' means carry it, but the comparison is about deaths.
Another meaning of the word: 'it takes time' means need; it does not fit hunters.
Another meaning of the word: 'take an offer' means accept; it does not fit the context.
Correct. Hunters 'take' animals by killing them, which matches the comparison with road deaths.

questions.q: According to paragraph 2, why do the researchers believe the real number of deaths is higher than their figures?
opts: Many dead animals are eaten by predators before anyone records them.
Their data cover only about half of California's roads.
Road workers are not allowed to report dead animals.
The database includes records of mammal species only.
questions.why: The researchers say their figures are underestimates 'since the data cover only around half of California's roads'.
questions.evidence: since the data cover only around half of California's roads
optWhy: Not mentioned: the passage gives no such reason.
Correct. It paraphrases 'the data cover only around half of California's roads'.
Not mentioned: the passage says observers do report dead animals.
Contradicts the passage: the database covers amphibians, birds, reptiles and mammals.

questions.q: According to paragraph 4, all of the following are true EXCEPT
opts: Collisions are concentrated on particular sections of several major highways.
Mountain lion populations on the southern and central coast are small.
Southern mountain lions have recently been removed from the threatened list.
Highways can separate lions into small groups that are isolated from each other.
questions.why: The paragraph says these populations have recently been listed as threatened, not removed from the list.
questions.evidence: have recently been listed as threatened under the California Endangered Species Act
optWhy: True: the report 'identifies hotspots where collisions cluster'.
True: 'mountain lion populations are small' in these areas.
Correct. This contradicts the passage: the populations were recently listed as threatened.
True: lions can 'become trapped in shrinking, isolated groups'.

questions.q: What can be inferred from paragraph 6 about the Wallis Annenberg Wildlife Crossing?
opts: It may work less well unless nearby areas are also fenced.
Animals have so far refused to use it.
It was designed and built without any advice from wildlife scientists.
It will replace the Liberty Canyon underpass.
questions.why: The report says bridges do not guarantee use without fences, and it names the underpass right next to the new crossing as a fencing priority. This suggests the crossing's success also depends on fencing nearby.
questions.evidence: It even names the Liberty Canyon underpass, right next to the new crossing, as a priority for fencing.
optWhy: Correct. Shilling's point and the Liberty Canyon example imply that the crossing needs fencing to be fully effective.
Contradicts the passage: paragraph 5 says a coyote has already used it.
Not mentioned: nothing is said about how it was designed.
Not supported: the underpass is a fencing priority, not something to be replaced.

questions.q: Why does the author mention that wildlife-vehicle collisions cost California at least $1 billion over five years?
opts: To show that fences are far too expensive for most transport agencies to build
To criticise transport agencies for wasting money on roads
To prove that most collisions involve mountain lions
To suggest that fencing's cost must be weighed against collision costs
questions.why: After noting that fencing costs money, the author uses 'Yet collisions have costs too' and the $1 billion figure to show that doing nothing is also expensive.
optWhy: Reversed: the figure is used to balance the cost of fencing, not to reject it.
Not supported: the author only says agencies 'might prefer' to spend on roads.
Not mentioned: the figure covers all large-animal collisions, not mainly mountain lions.
Correct. 'Yet collisions have costs too' introduces a comparison of the two costs.

questions.q: Which of the sentences below best expresses the essential information in the highlighted sentence in paragraph 4? Incorrect choices change the meaning in important ways or leave out essential information.
opts: Crossing often kills lions, and staying put can leave them in small, cut-off groups with less genetic variety.
Lions that stay behind on one side of the highway are killed more often than lions that try to cross the road.
Lions lose genetic diversity mainly because they cross highways too often.
Isolated groups of lions are growing because fewer lions now try to cross.
questions.why: The sentence describes two separate dangers: lions that cross are killed, and lions that stay become isolated and lose genetic diversity. Only A keeps both.
questions.evidence: Lions that try to cross are often killed, while those that stay behind can become trapped in shrinking, isolated groups that lose genetic diversity.
optWhy: Correct. It keeps both dangers: death when crossing and isolation when staying.
Reversed: the passage says crossing lions are the ones often killed.
Cause reversed: genetic diversity is lost because lions cannot cross, not because they cross.
Contradicts the passage: the groups are 'shrinking', not growing.
questions.highlight: Lions that try to cross are often killed, while those that stay behind can become trapped in shrinking, isolated groups that lose genetic diversity.

write.p: Professor: A new report says vehicles kill about 18% of California's mountain lions each year. Some people want governments to build more large wildlife bridges, like the new crossing near Los Angeles. Others say long stretches of simple fencing would save more animals for less money. If your local government had a limited budget to reduce roadkill, which would you spend it on, and why? (Sophie says: I would build a wildlife bridge. A big, visible project gets people talking and shows that the city cares about nature. That public support can bring in more donations for other projects later.) (Kevin says: I would choose fencing. The report says fencing is the real answer and that bridges do not guarantee animals will use them. Fences next to existing tunnels could protect far more animals for the same money.)
steps: Pick one option: a wildlife bridge or fencing.
Give one reason based on the report's evidence.
Add an example, such as the Liberty Canyon underpass or the 780 lions killed each year.
Respond to Sophie or Kevin and conclude.
